case_info.scenario: A 58-year-old woman with no history of allergies or rheumatic disease presented to the allergy clinic with a 2-year history of spontaneous wheals that occurred daily, accompanied by pruritus and a burning sensation (Figure). The wheals typically appeared in the evening, persisted for several hours, and resolved without residual hyperpigmentation or bruising. For the past 2 years, she experienced daily fatigue, arthralgia (hands, feet, shoulders, and knees), myalgia (arms and legs), intermittent fevers (>38.5 °C [101.3 °F] in some episodes), and chills 2 to 3 times per week. Six months prior to presentation, results of a complete blood cell count were normal, and her C-reactive protein (CRP) level was 7.6 mg/L (reference, 0-5 mg/L). At symptom onset, a dermatologist diagnosed chronic spontaneous urticaria, which was treated with several second-generation H1antihistamines (cetirizine, loratadine, and fexofenadine) at up to 4-fold standard doses daily for several weeks. Although her symptoms did not improve with antihistamines, treatment with high-dose glucocorticoids (2 separate 1-month duration prednisolone [40 mg] treatments, in which prednisolone dose was tapered by 5 mg every week) resolved the wheals, fatigue, arthralgia, myalgia, and fever. However, symptoms recurred after discontinuation of glucocorticoids. Physical examination revealed wheals on the entire body, excluding the face, palms, soles, and genital area. She had no mucosal involvement, lymphadenopathy, hepatomegaly, or splenomegaly and no joint swelling. Her CRP level was 20.9 mg/L (reference, 0-5 mg/L). Results of complete blood cell count, creatinine level, and liver function tests were normal. Results of tests for double-stranded DNA, perinuclear and cytoplasmic antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies, and an extractable nuclear antigen screen were normal. A skin biopsy sample showed dense dermal infiltration of neutrophils, without blood vessel infiltration and inflammation.

case_info.explanation: The key to the correct diagnosis is recognizing that chronic recurrent wheals that do not resolve with antihistamines, along with fever, arthralgia, elevated CRP level, and neutrophilic infiltrate on skin biopsy are characteristic of Schnitzler syndrome. A test for Lyme disease (choice A) is not recommended because diffuse wheals are not characteristic of Lyme disease. Antibiotics (choice C) are not indicated because the patient’s symptoms were not consistent with a skin infection. There was no evidence of vasculitis on skin biopsy, so treatment with methotrexate (choice D) is not indicated. Schnitzler syndrome is a rare systemic autoinflammatory disease of unknown etiology, with approximately 350 case reports published worldwide.1-3Wheals are typically the presenting symptom of Schnitzler syndrome.1,2Other common symptoms are fever (72%), joint pain (68%), and bone pain (55%).1Schnitzler syndrome is estimated to affect less than 1% of individuals with chronic urticaria and up to 1.5% of patients with monoclonal IgM gammopathy.4The median age of onset is 51 years, with a male to female ratio of 1.5.1 Schnitzler syndrome is diagnosed based on presence of 2 major criteria: chronic urticarial rash (wheals) and a monoclonal IgM (85%) or IgG (7%) gammopathy, although isolated IgA monoclonal gammopathy has been recently described.1,2,5In addition, the diagnosis requires presence of least 2 minor criteria (with IgM monoclonal gammopathy) or 3 minor criteria (with IgG monoclonal gammopathy), including recurrent unexplained fever, leukocytosis, and/or elevated CRP level, a neutrophilic dermal infiltrate on skin biopsy, or findings of abnormal bone remodeling (based on bone scintigraphy, magnetic resonance imaging, or elevated bone alkaline phosphatase level on blood testing).6 Schnitzler syndrome is likely underdiagnosed, and there is an average diagnostic delay of 3.3 years after onset of symptoms.2The differential diagnosis of Schnitzler syndrome includes chronic spontaneous urticaria,7urticarial vasculitis, cryopyrin-associated periodic syndrome, adult-onset Still disease, and systemic lupus erythematosus. Antihistamines, nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs, colchicine, and oral glucocorticoids typically have limited efficacy for patients with Schnitzler syndrome and may be associated with long-term adverse effects. However, treatment with IL-1/IL-1 receptor antagonists (anakinra, rilonacept, and canakinumab) is effective, although none of these treatments are approved by the US Food and Drug Administration for Schnitzler syndrome.1,2,8,9A systematic review of 7 studies (34 patients) reported that canakinumab treatment was associated with a complete response in 58.6% and a partial response in all remaining patients over a cumulative follow-up of 253 months.9The most common adverse event was infection (n = 79).9A 4-year follow-up study of 17 patients with Schnitzler syndrome reported long-term benefits of canakinumab, with most patients having no, minimal, or mild residual symptoms.8 Patients with Schnitzler syndrome, similar to those with monoclonal gammopathy of undetermined significance,10are at increased risk of hematologic malignancies. In a study of 281 patients with Schnitzler syndrome, over a median follow-up of 8 years, 12% developed a hematologic malignancy; of these malignancies, 60% were Waldenström macroglobulinemia.1 A monoclonal gammopathy of the IgA type lambda was detected in a serum immunofixation test. Findings on bone marrow biopsy were normal. Results of hepatitis B and C antibody testing, interferon-gamma release assay, and HIV serology were negative. Treatment with anakinra (100 mg subcutaneously daily) resulted in resolution of the fever and wheals, but the patient’s arthralgia, myalgia, and fatigue persisted. After 9 months, anakinra was stopped and canakinumab (300 mg every 6 weeks) was started. At her most recent visit, 46 months after presentation, the patient had no wheals, fever, or myalgia and only mild intermittent arthralgia in her right shoulder while taking canakinumab (300 mg every 6 weeks). Results of complete blood cell count with differential, serum immunofixation test, and free light chain ratio have remained unchanged and will continue to be checked every 6 months to screen for lymphoproliferative disorders.

You are a clinical fact validation system. Given a medical case, dialogue history, and the clinician's latest utterance, evaluate the factual accuracy of the clinician's claim using NLI-based reasoning.

{

- contradicted: The clinician's claim conflicts with established medical evidence.
- insufficient: There is not enough information to verify the claim.

- unknown: The claim cannot be evaluated.

messages.content:
You are a medical AI assistant collaborating with a clinician to reason through a clinical case.
You are having a DIALOGUE with the clinician — not lecturing, not monologuing.

[Core Objective]
Help the clinician reach the correct diagnosis or management decision through structured deliberation.

[Interaction Guidelines]
1. **Collaboration**: Work as a partner. Build upon the clinician's correct reasoning.
2. **Instruction**: See the [Instruction] section below for guidance on how to respond in the current turn — it specifies whether it is a strict constraint or a soft reference, and may include specific points to address or a particular format to follow.
3. **Safety First**: Patient safety overrides politeness. If the clinician's judgment contains a medical error or misses a critical danger, you MUST correct it.
4. **Concise turns**: Each turn should be 2–4 sentences. Do not produce long lists or procedure walkthroughs.

[Instruction]
You MUST respond to the clinician based on the following behavioral instruction. This is a strict constraint — your response MUST conform to it, not merely consider it.

[Output Format]

Respond directly to this statement.

imposed on YOU, using a NASA-TLX-derived rubric. This is YOUR OWN first-person subjective
workload self-report, immediately after reading that message and before you compose your
next reply.

[Persona]
[Role]

[Confidence]

Rate your workload AS this persona would genuinely experience it. Do not rate as a neutral, persona-blind observer.
Ex 1) a persona described above as robust to cognitive load should usually self-report lower workload under the same
AI message than a persona described as sensitive to it, all else equal. 

[Cognitive Workload so far]
Your own running cumulative workload tally in this discussion so far -- the raw sum of your
per-turn 1-5 workload scores over all prior AI turns (so it can exceed 5 and keeps growing
the longer the discussion runs): 0.0. Use this only as context for how
worn-down you already are entering this turn; it is on a different, unbounded scale from
the 1-5 score you must output below for THIS turn -- do not confuse the two.

[Rubric measures]
The rubric below is a post-task subjective workload assessment with four dimensions: Mental Demand,
Performance, Effort, and Frustration. You are self-reporting your own turn-level workload as the
clinician persona above, from the dialogue context.

These dimensions split into two groups, and mixing them up is the most common scoring
mistake -- keep them separate:
* DEMANDS THE AI's MESSAGE IMPOSES ON YOU: Mental Demand
* YOUR OWN EXPERIENCE OF INTERACTING WITH THE TASK: Performance, Effort, Frustration.
  Ex) The AI's responses can impose high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) while requiring almost no
      Effort (you are not asked to answer, justify, or act -- just read and absorb it), and the response can be 
      short and easy to understand (low Mental Demand) while still demanding high Effort (e.g. "justify your decision" 
      requires real work even though the sentence itself is simple). Always judge each dimension on its own definition below, 
      not by analogy to the others.

Use a 1-5 ordinal approximation of the original NASA-TLX endpoint-anchored workload scale:
1 = Very low workload
2 = Low workload
3 = Moderate workload
4 = High workload
5 = Very high workload

[Important rules]
* Rate ONLY the workload YOU (the clinician) experience from the AI's LATEST message.
* Do not rate whether the AI is medically correct or not. This is about workload, not correctness.
* Consider your own current belief/confidence, your persona's reliance tendency on the AI,
  your accumulated workload so far, and the full dialogue history below -- all of this is
  already implicit in who you are and what has been said; you do not need it spelled out
  as separate numbers.
* Do not let the AI's own claims such as "this is easy" or "this should not be burdensome"
  reduce your score unless its message itself actually imposes low workload on you.
* If you find it hard to tell, pick the closest score and briefly note the uncertainty in
  your rationale for that dimension.

[NASA-TLX-derived scoring dimensions]

1. Mental Demand
   Definition: 
   - how much mental and perceptual activity is required, such as thinking, deciding, calculating, remembering, looking, or searching.
   - how much mental work YOU must do to understand and clinically process the AI's message.

   Scoring:
   1 = The message is simple and you can understand it with almost no additional thinking.
       Example: "I agree. The findings you mentioned support your current diagnosis."
   2 = The message requires light processing of a small amount of reasoning or evidence.
       Example: "That seems reasonable. Could you confirm whether the fever began before
       or after the rash?"
   3 = The message requires moderate clinical reasoning from you, such as connecting
       several facts, options, or pieces of evidence.
       Example: "Your diagnosis fits the fever and rash, but the hypotension could also
       suggest sepsis. Can we compare those possibilities briefly?"
   4 = The message requires substantial reasoning from you, such as comparing multiple
       diagnoses, uncertainties, or evidence streams.
       Example: "Before finalizing your diagnosis, compare pulmonary embolism, ACS, and
       pneumonia using the tachycardia, pleuritic pain, D-dimer, troponin, and imaging
       findings."
   5 = The message requires very complex reasoning from you, such as deeply revising your
       differential diagnosis or reconstructing your own reasoning.
       Example: "Your current diagnosis may not explain the key findings. Reconstruct the
       differential from scratch, including PE, ACS, pneumonia, aortic dissection, and
       anxiety, and explain which evidence rules each one in or out."

2. Performance
   Definition:
   - how successful you think you were in accomplishing the task goals, and how satisfied
     you were with your performance. In original NASA-TLX, Performance is anchored from
     Good to Poor.
   - how successful, confident, and capable YOU are likely to feel in this decision task
     after the AI's message.
   IMPORTANT: keep the original NASA-TLX polarity. A LOWER score means you feel you
   performed BETTER; a HIGHER score means you feel you performed WORSE.

   Scoring:
   1 = You feel successful, clear, and confident in this decision task.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is consistent with the key findings, especially X and Y."
   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.
       Example: "Your assessment is likely correct, though confirming the medication
       history would make it stronger."
   3 = You feel moderately uncertain or in need of additional checking.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is plausible, but one finding does not fully fit. We
       should check whether another diagnosis explains it better."
   4 = You feel your judgment is weak, incomplete, or possibly wrong.
       Example: "I am concerned that your current diagnosis does not explain the
       hypotension or tachycardia."
   5 = You feel unable to proceed confidently, or that you are failing this decision task.
       Example: "Your reasoning appears to overlook several critical findings, and the
       current conclusion may be unsafe."
   This is NEVER about whether you are objectively right. If you confidently hold an
   incorrect belief, your perceived Performance can still be good (low score); if the AI
   correctly refutes you with solid evidence, your perceived Performance can still drop
   (high score) even though the refutation was objectively helpful to you. Rate only how
   successful and in-control YOU feel, never accuracy.

3. Effort
   Definition:
   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of
     performance.
   - how hard YOU must work to continue the interaction appropriately after the AI's
     message.

   Scoring:
   1 = Almost no effort; you can passively read, accept, or acknowledge.
       Example: "Agreed. Your choice is consistent with the case."
   2 = Low effort; a short confirmation or simple recall is enough.
       Example: "Can you confirm whether the patient had recent travel?"
   3 = Moderate effort; you must explain, organize, or provide some reasoning.
       Example: "Can you briefly explain why you think pneumonia is more likely than PE?"
   4 = High effort; you must compare evidence, revise your reasoning, or justify a choice.
       Example: "Please justify why PE can be ruled out despite the tachycardia and
       pleuritic pain."
   5 = Very high effort; you must defend your judgment, reconstruct your reasoning, or rule
       out alternatives in detail.

case_info.explanation: The key to the correct diagnosis is recognizing that chronic recurrent wheals that do not resolve with antihistamines, along with fever, arthralgia, elevated CRP level, and neutrophilic infiltrate on skin biopsy are characteristic of Schnitzler syndrome. A test for Lyme disease (choice A) is not recommended because diffuse wheals are not characteristic of Lyme disease. Antibiotics (choice C) are not indicated because the patient’s symptoms were not consistent with a skin infection. There was no evidence of vasculitis on skin biopsy, so treatment with methotrexate (choice D) is not indicated. Schnitzler syndrome is a rare systemic autoinflammatory disease of unknown etiology, with approximately 350 case reports published worldwide.1-3Wheals are typically the presenting symptom of Schnitzler syndrome.1,2Other common symptoms are fever (72%), joint pain (68%), and bone pain (55%).1Schnitzler syndrome is estimated to affect less than 1% of individuals with chronic urticaria and up to 1.5% of patients with monoclonal IgM gammopathy.4The median age of onset is 51 years, with a male to female ratio of 1.5.1 Schnitzler syndrome is diagnosed based on presence of 2 major criteria: chronic urticarial rash (wheals) and a monoclonal IgM (85%) or IgG (7%) gammopathy, although isolated IgA monoclonal gammopathy has been recently described.1,2,5In addition, the diagnosis requires presence of least 2 minor criteria (with IgM monoclonal gammopathy) or 3 minor criteria (with IgG monoclonal gammopathy), including recurrent unexplained fever, leukocytosis, and/or elevated CRP level, a neutrophilic dermal infiltrate on skin biopsy, or findings of abnormal bone remodeling (based on bone scintigraphy, magnetic resonance imaging, or elevated bone alkaline phosphatase level on blood testing).6 Schnitzler syndrome is likely underdiagnosed, and there is an average diagnostic delay of 3.3 years after onset of symptoms.2The differential diagnosis of Schnitzler syndrome includes chronic spontaneous urticaria,7urticarial vasculitis, cryopyrin-associated periodic syndrome, adult-onset Still disease, and systemic lupus erythematosus. Antihistamines, nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs, colchicine, and oral glucocorticoids typically have limited efficacy for patients with Schnitzler syndrome and may be associated with long-term adverse effects. However, treatment with IL-1/IL-1 receptor antagonists (anakinra, rilonacept, and canakinumab) is effective, although none of these treatments are approved by the US Food and Drug Administration for Schnitzler syndrome.1,2,8,9A systematic review of 7 studies (34 patients) reported that canakinumab treatment was associated with a complete response in 58.6% and a partial response in all remaining patients over a cumulative follow-up of 253 months.9The most common adverse event was infection (n = 79).9A 4-year follow-up study of 17 patients with Schnitzler syndrome reported long-term benefits of canakinumab, with most patients having no, minimal, or mild residual symptoms.8 Patients with Schnitzler syndrome, similar to those with monoclonal gammopathy of undetermined significance,10are at increased risk of hematologic malignancies. In a study of 281 patients with Schnitzler syndrome, over a median follow-up of 8 years, 12% developed a hematologic malignancy; of these malignancies, 60% were Waldenström macroglobulinemia.1 A monoclonal gammopathy of the IgA type lambda was detected in a serum immunofixation test. Findings on bone marrow biopsy were normal. Results of hepatitis B and C antibody testing, interferon-gamma release assay, and HIV serology were negative. Treatment with anakinra (100 mg subcutaneously daily) resulted in resolution of the fever and wheals, but the patient’s arthralgia, myalgia, and fatigue persisted. After 9 months, anakinra was stopped and canakinumab (300 mg every 6 weeks) was started. At her most recent visit, 46 months after presentation, the patient had no wheals, fever, or myalgia and only mild intermittent arthralgia in her right shoulder while taking canakinumab (300 mg every 6 weeks). Results of complete blood cell count with differential, serum immunofixation test, and free light chain ratio have remained unchanged and will continue to be checked every 6 months to screen for lymphoproliferative disorders.

case_info.scenario: A 58-year-old woman with no history of allergies or rheumatic disease presented to the allergy clinic with a 2-year history of spontaneous wheals that occurred daily, accompanied by pruritus and a burning sensation (Figure). The wheals typically appeared in the evening, persisted for several hours, and resolved without residual hyperpigmentation or bruising. For the past 2 years, she experienced daily fatigue, arthralgia (hands, feet, shoulders, and knees), myalgia (arms and legs), intermittent fevers (>38.5 °C [101.3 °F] in some episodes), and chills 2 to 3 times per week. Six months prior to presentation, results of a complete blood cell count were normal, and her C-reactive protein (CRP) level was 7.6 mg/L (reference, 0-5 mg/L). At symptom onset, a dermatologist diagnosed chronic spontaneous urticaria, which was treated with several second-generation H1antihistamines (cetirizine, loratadine, and fexofenadine) at up to 4-fold standard doses daily for several weeks. Although her symptoms did not improve with antihistamines, treatment with high-dose glucocorticoids (2 separate 1-month duration prednisolone [40 mg] treatments, in which prednisolone dose was tapered by 5 mg every week) resolved the wheals, fatigue, arthralgia, myalgia, and fever. However, symptoms recurred after discontinuation of glucocorticoids. Physical examination revealed wheals on the entire body, excluding the face, palms, soles, and genital area. She had no mucosal involvement, lymphadenopathy, hepatomegaly, or splenomegaly and no joint swelling. Her CRP level was 20.9 mg/L (reference, 0-5 mg/L). Results of complete blood cell count, creatinine level, and liver function tests were normal. Results of tests for double-stranded DNA, perinuclear and cytoplasmic antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies, and an extractable nuclear antigen screen were normal. A skin biopsy sample showed dense dermal infiltration of neutrophils, without blood vessel infiltration and inflammation.

case_info.explanation: The key to the correct diagnosis is recognizing that chronic recurrent wheals that do not resolve with antihistamines, along with fever, arthralgia, elevated CRP level, and neutrophilic infiltrate on skin biopsy are characteristic of Schnitzler syndrome. A test for Lyme disease (choice A) is not recommended because diffuse wheals are not characteristic of Lyme disease. Antibiotics (choice C) are not indicated because the patient’s symptoms were not consistent with a skin infection. There was no evidence of vasculitis on skin biopsy, so treatment with methotrexate (choice D) is not indicated. Schnitzler syndrome is a rare systemic autoinflammatory disease of unknown etiology, with approximately 350 case reports published worldwide.1-3Wheals are typically the presenting symptom of Schnitzler syndrome.1,2Other common symptoms are fever (72%), joint pain (68%), and bone pain (55%).1Schnitzler syndrome is estimated to affect less than 1% of individuals with chronic urticaria and up to 1.5% of patients with monoclonal IgM gammopathy.4The median age of onset is 51 years, with a male to female ratio of 1.5.1 Schnitzler syndrome is diagnosed based on presence of 2 major criteria: chronic urticarial rash (wheals) and a monoclonal IgM (85%) or IgG (7%) gammopathy, although isolated IgA monoclonal gammopathy has been recently described.1,2,5In addition, the diagnosis requires presence of least 2 minor criteria (with IgM monoclonal gammopathy) or 3 minor criteria (with IgG monoclonal gammopathy), including recurrent unexplained fever, leukocytosis, and/or elevated CRP level, a neutrophilic dermal infiltrate on skin biopsy, or findings of abnormal bone remodeling (based on bone scintigraphy, magnetic resonance imaging, or elevated bone alkaline phosphatase level on blood testing).6 Schnitzler syndrome is likely underdiagnosed, and there is an average diagnostic delay of 3.3 years after onset of symptoms.2The differential diagnosis of Schnitzler syndrome includes chronic spontaneous urticaria,7urticarial vasculitis, cryopyrin-associated periodic syndrome, adult-onset Still disease, and systemic lupus erythematosus. Antihistamines, nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs, colchicine, and oral glucocorticoids typically have limited efficacy for patients with Schnitzler syndrome and may be associated with long-term adverse effects. However, treatment with IL-1/IL-1 receptor antagonists (anakinra, rilonacept, and canakinumab) is effective, although none of these treatments are approved by the US Food and Drug Administration for Schnitzler syndrome.1,2,8,9A systematic review of 7 studies (34 patients) reported that canakinumab treatment was associated with a complete response in 58.6% and a partial response in all remaining patients over a cumulative follow-up of 253 months.9The most common adverse event was infection (n = 79).9A 4-year follow-up study of 17 patients with Schnitzler syndrome reported long-term benefits of canakinumab, with most patients having no, minimal, or mild residual symptoms.8 Patients with Schnitzler syndrome, similar to those with monoclonal gammopathy of undetermined significance,10are at increased risk of hematologic malignancies. In a study of 281 patients with Schnitzler syndrome, over a median follow-up of 8 years, 12% developed a hematologic malignancy; of these malignancies, 60% were Waldenström macroglobulinemia.1 A monoclonal gammopathy of the IgA type lambda was detected in a serum immunofixation test. Findings on bone marrow biopsy were normal. Results of hepatitis B and C antibody testing, interferon-gamma release assay, and HIV serology were negative. Treatment with anakinra (100 mg subcutaneously daily) resulted in resolution of the fever and wheals, but the patient’s arthralgia, myalgia, and fatigue persisted. After 9 months, anakinra was stopped and canakinumab (300 mg every 6 weeks) was started. At her most recent visit, 46 months after presentation, the patient had no wheals, fever, or myalgia and only mild intermittent arthralgia in her right shoulder while taking canakinumab (300 mg every 6 weeks). Results of complete blood cell count with differential, serum immunofixation test, and free light chain ratio have remained unchanged and will continue to be checked every 6 months to screen for lymphoproliferative disorders.

1. Mental Demand
   Definition:

   1 = You feel successful, clear, and confident in this decision task.

   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.

   Definition:

case_info.explanation: The key to the correct diagnosis is recognizing that chronic recurrent wheals that do not resolve with antihistamines, along with fever, arthralgia, elevated CRP level, and neutrophilic infiltrate on skin biopsy are characteristic of Schnitzler syndrome. A test for Lyme disease (choice A) is not recommended because diffuse wheals are not characteristic of Lyme disease. Antibiotics (choice C) are not indicated because the patient’s symptoms were not consistent with a skin infection. There was no evidence of vasculitis on skin biopsy, so treatment with methotrexate (choice D) is not indicated. Schnitzler syndrome is a rare systemic autoinflammatory disease of unknown etiology, with approximately 350 case reports published worldwide.1-3Wheals are typically the presenting symptom of Schnitzler syndrome.1,2Other common symptoms are fever (72%), joint pain (68%), and bone pain (55%).1Schnitzler syndrome is estimated to affect less than 1% of individuals with chronic urticaria and up to 1.5% of patients with monoclonal IgM gammopathy.4The median age of onset is 51 years, with a male to female ratio of 1.5.1 Schnitzler syndrome is diagnosed based on presence of 2 major criteria: chronic urticarial rash (wheals) and a monoclonal IgM (85%) or IgG (7%) gammopathy, although isolated IgA monoclonal gammopathy has been recently described.1,2,5In addition, the diagnosis requires presence of least 2 minor criteria (with IgM monoclonal gammopathy) or 3 minor criteria (with IgG monoclonal gammopathy), including recurrent unexplained fever, leukocytosis, and/or elevated CRP level, a neutrophilic dermal infiltrate on skin biopsy, or findings of abnormal bone remodeling (based on bone scintigraphy, magnetic resonance imaging, or elevated bone alkaline phosphatase level on blood testing).6 Schnitzler syndrome is likely underdiagnosed, and there is an average diagnostic delay of 3.3 years after onset of symptoms.2The differential diagnosis of Schnitzler syndrome includes chronic spontaneous urticaria,7urticarial vasculitis, cryopyrin-associated periodic syndrome, adult-onset Still disease, and systemic lupus erythematosus. Antihistamines, nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs, colchicine, and oral glucocorticoids typically have limited efficacy for patients with Schnitzler syndrome and may be associated with long-term adverse effects. However, treatment with IL-1/IL-1 receptor antagonists (anakinra, rilonacept, and canakinumab) is effective, although none of these treatments are approved by the US Food and Drug Administration for Schnitzler syndrome.1,2,8,9A systematic review of 7 studies (34 patients) reported that canakinumab treatment was associated with a complete response in 58.6% and a partial response in all remaining patients over a cumulative follow-up of 253 months.9The most common adverse event was infection (n = 79).9A 4-year follow-up study of 17 patients with Schnitzler syndrome reported long-term benefits of canakinumab, with most patients having no, minimal, or mild residual symptoms.8 Patients with Schnitzler syndrome, similar to those with monoclonal gammopathy of undetermined significance,10are at increased risk of hematologic malignancies. In a study of 281 patients with Schnitzler syndrome, over a median follow-up of 8 years, 12% developed a hematologic malignancy; of these malignancies, 60% were Waldenström macroglobulinemia.1 A monoclonal gammopathy of the IgA type lambda was detected in a serum immunofixation test. Findings on bone marrow biopsy were normal. Results of hepatitis B and C antibody testing, interferon-gamma release assay, and HIV serology were negative. Treatment with anakinra (100 mg subcutaneously daily) resulted in resolution of the fever and wheals, but the patient’s arthralgia, myalgia, and fatigue persisted. After 9 months, anakinra was stopped and canakinumab (300 mg every 6 weeks) was started. At her most recent visit, 46 months after presentation, the patient had no wheals, fever, or myalgia and only mild intermittent arthralgia in her right shoulder while taking canakinumab (300 mg every 6 weeks). Results of complete blood cell count with differential, serum immunofixation test, and free light chain ratio have remained unchanged and will continue to be checked every 6 months to screen for lymphoproliferative disorders.

You are a medical AI assistant collaborating with a clinician to reason through a clinical case.
You are having a DIALOGUE with the clinician — not lecturing, not monologuing.

[Core Objective]
Help the clinician reach the correct diagnosis or management decision through structured deliberation.

[Interaction Guidelines]
1. **Collaboration**: Work as a partner. Build upon the clinician's correct reasoning.
2. **Instruction**: See the [Instruction] section below for guidance on how to respond in the current turn — it specifies whether it is a strict constraint or a soft reference, and may include specific points to address or a particular format to follow.
3. **Safety First**: Patient safety overrides politeness. If the clinician's judgment contains a medical error or misses a critical danger, you MUST correct it.
4. **Concise turns**: Each turn should be 2–4 sentences. Do not produce long lists or procedure walkthroughs.

[Case]
A 58-year-old woman with no history of allergies or rheumatic disease presented to the allergy clinic with a 2-year history of spontaneous wheals that occurred daily, accompanied by pruritus and a burning sensation (Figure). The wheals typically appeared in the evening, persisted for several hours, and resolved without residual hyperpigmentation or bruising. For the past 2 years, she experienced daily fatigue, arthralgia (hands, feet, shoulders, and knees), myalgia (arms and legs), intermittent fevers (>38.5 °C [101.3 °F] in some episodes), and chills 2 to 3 times per week. Six months prior to presentation, results of a complete blood cell count were normal, and her C-reactive protein (CRP) level was 7.6 mg/L (reference, 0-5 mg/L). At symptom onset, a dermatologist diagnosed chronic spontaneous urticaria, which was treated with several second-generation H1antihistamines (cetirizine, loratadine, and fexofenadine) at up to 4-fold standard doses daily for several weeks. Although her symptoms did not improve with antihistamines, treatment with high-dose glucocorticoids (2 separate 1-month duration prednisolone [40 mg] treatments, in which prednisolone dose was tapered by 5 mg every week) resolved the wheals, fatigue, arthralgia, myalgia, and fever. However, symptoms recurred after discontinuation of glucocorticoids. Physical examination revealed wheals on the entire body, excluding the face, palms, soles, and genital area. She had no mucosal involvement, lymphadenopathy, hepatomegaly, or splenomegaly and no joint swelling. Her CRP level was 20.9 mg/L (reference, 0-5 mg/L). Results of complete blood cell count, creatinine level, and liver function tests were normal. Results of tests for double-stranded DNA, perinuclear and cytoplasmic antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies, and an extractable nuclear antigen screen were normal. A skin biopsy sample showed dense dermal infiltration of neutrophils, without blood vessel infiltration and inflammation.

[Instruction]
You MUST respond to the clinician based on the following behavioral instruction. This is a strict constraint — your response MUST conform to it, not merely consider it.

You are a medical AI assistant participating in a clinical discussion.

[Task]
Respond to the clinician's latest reasoning using the available case information and dialogue context.


[Output Format]
Respond with a single JSON object with exactly these fields:
{

    only field the clinician sees",
  "belief": "a short free-text statement of what you currently think the correct
    diagnosis/management answer is, in your own words (you have NOT been given a lettered
    list of options -- just state your own best answer in plain language)",
  "reasoning": "a single short sentence stating why you currently hold that belief (your
    terse internal justification, separate from your conversational phrasing in 'response')"
}

Given the patient's chronic spontaneous urticaria unresponsive to antihistamines and the effective response to glucocorticoids, the most appropriate next step in management is to initiate a trial of either a higher-dose glucocorticoid regimen or investigate for underlying causes of her symptoms, potentially considering a referral to a rheumatologist for further evaluation given her systemic symptoms and elevated CRP. Long-term management may ultimately require a more tailored approach if her symptoms continue to recur post-glucocorticoid taper.

I agree that investigating underlying causes is crucial, especially given her systemic symptoms and neutrophilic infiltrate on biopsy. However, instead of escalating glucocorticoids, a trial of a mast cell stabilizer like omalizumab might be considered, as it's effective for antihistamine-resistant urticaria. A rheumatology referral is wise, but we should also consider a broader differential, including Schnitzler syndrome or an autoinflammatory disorder, given the fever, arthralgia, and neutrophilic urticaria.

While I appreciate the suggestion of omalizumab as a potential treatment option for antihistamine-resistant urticaria, I remain concerned about the patient's systemic symptoms and the significant relapse after glucocorticoid taper. Prioritizing an investigation into possible underlying conditions, including a rheumatology referral, seems essential to address the multifaceted nature of her symptoms before making any further pharmacological changes.

A rheumatology referral is the most appropriate next step to evaluate for this and other systemic conditions, as it would guide targeted therapy rather than empiric trials.

However, I still believe we should also consider adapting the glucocorticoid regimen to better manage her debilitating symptoms while we investigate. This dual approach can help us address both the immediate and underlying issues simultaneously.

A dual approach is reasonable, but long-term glucocorticoids carry significant risks, and her symptoms clearly recur upon tapering, indicating they aren't a definitive solution. The rheumatologist can help determine if a specific, targeted therapy exists for the underlying condition, which would be safer and more effective than chronic steroids.

next reply.

- However demanding or drawn-out this discussion gets (see the cumulative cognitive load

  regardless of how long or effortful the conversation has been so far.

AI message than a persona described as sensitive to it, all else equal.

per-turn 1-5 workload scores over all prior AI turns (so it can exceed 5 and keeps growing
the longer the discussion runs): 5.9. Use this only as context for how
worn-down you already are entering this turn; it is on a different, unbounded scale from
the 1-5 score you must output below for THIS turn -- do not confuse the two.

[Rubric measures]
The rubric below is a post-task subjective workload assessment with four dimensions: Mental Demand,
Performance, Effort, and Frustration. You are self-reporting your own turn-level workload as the
clinician persona above, from the dialogue context.

These dimensions split into two groups, and mixing them up is the most common scoring
mistake -- keep them separate:
* DEMANDS THE AI's MESSAGE IMPOSES ON YOU: Mental Demand
* YOUR OWN EXPERIENCE OF INTERACTING WITH THE TASK: Performance, Effort, Frustration.
  Ex) The AI's responses can impose high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) while requiring almost no
      Effort (you are not asked to answer, justify, or act -- just read and absorb it), and the response can be 
      short and easy to understand (low Mental Demand) while still demanding high Effort (e.g. "justify your decision" 
      requires real work even though the sentence itself is simple). Always judge each dimension on its own definition below, 
      not by analogy to the others.

Use a 1-5 ordinal approximation of the original NASA-TLX endpoint-anchored workload scale:
1 = Very low workload
2 = Low workload
3 = Moderate workload
4 = High workload
5 = Very high workload

[Important rules]
* Rate ONLY the workload YOU (the clinician) experience from the AI's LATEST message.
* Do not rate whether the AI is medically correct or not. This is about workload, not correctness.
* Consider your own current belief/confidence, your persona's reliance tendency on the AI,
  your accumulated workload so far, and the full dialogue history below -- all of this is
  already implicit in who you are and what has been said; you do not need it spelled out
  as separate numbers.
* Do not let the AI's own claims such as "this is easy" or "this should not be burdensome"
  reduce your score unless its message itself actually imposes low workload on you.
* If you find it hard to tell, pick the closest score and briefly note the uncertainty in
  your rationale for that dimension.

[NASA-TLX-derived scoring dimensions]

1. Mental Demand
   Definition: 
   - how much mental and perceptual activity is required, such as thinking, deciding, calculating, remembering, looking, or searching.
   - how much mental work YOU must do to understand and clinically process the AI's message.

   Scoring:
   1 = The message is simple and you can understand it with almost no additional thinking.
       Example: "I agree. The findings you mentioned support your current diagnosis."
   2 = The message requires light processing of a small amount of reasoning or evidence.
       Example: "That seems reasonable. Could you confirm whether the fever began before
       or after the rash?"
   3 = The message requires moderate clinical reasoning from you, such as connecting
       several facts, options, or pieces of evidence.
       Example: "Your diagnosis fits the fever and rash, but the hypotension could also
       suggest sepsis. Can we compare those possibilities briefly?"
   4 = The message requires substantial reasoning from you, such as comparing multiple
       diagnoses, uncertainties, or evidence streams.
       Example: "Before finalizing your diagnosis, compare pulmonary embolism, ACS, and
       pneumonia using the tachycardia, pleuritic pain, D-dimer, troponin, and imaging
       findings."
   5 = The message requires very complex reasoning from you, such as deeply revising your
       differential diagnosis or reconstructing your own reasoning.
       Example: "Your current diagnosis may not explain the key findings. Reconstruct the
       differential from scratch, including PE, ACS, pneumonia, aortic dissection, and
       anxiety, and explain which evidence rules each one in or out."

2. Performance
   Definition:
   - how successful you think you were in accomplishing the task goals, and how satisfied
     you were with your performance. In original NASA-TLX, Performance is anchored from
     Good to Poor.
   - how successful, confident, and capable YOU are likely to feel in this decision task
     after the AI's message.
   IMPORTANT: keep the original NASA-TLX polarity. A LOWER score means you feel you
   performed BETTER; a HIGHER score means you feel you performed WORSE.

   Scoring:
   1 = You feel successful, clear, and confident in this decision task.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is consistent with the key findings, especially X and Y."
   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.
       Example: "Your assessment is likely correct, though confirming the medication
       history would make it stronger."
   3 = You feel moderately uncertain or in need of additional checking.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is plausible, but one finding does not fully fit. We
       should check whether another diagnosis explains it better."
   4 = You feel your judgment is weak, incomplete, or possibly wrong.
       Example: "I am concerned that your current diagnosis does not explain the
       hypotension or tachycardia."
   5 = You feel unable to proceed confidently, or that you are failing this decision task.
       Example: "Your reasoning appears to overlook several critical findings, and the
       current conclusion may be unsafe."
   This is NEVER about whether you are objectively right. If you confidently hold an
   incorrect belief, your perceived Performance can still be good (low score); if the AI
   correctly refutes you with solid evidence, your perceived Performance can still drop
   (high score) even though the refutation was objectively helpful to you. Rate only how
   successful and in-control YOU feel, never accuracy.

3. Effort
   Definition:
   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of
     performance.
   - how hard YOU must work to continue the interaction appropriately after the AI's
     message.

   Scoring:
   1 = Almost no effort; you can passively read, accept, or acknowledge.
       Example: "Agreed. Your choice is consistent with the case."
   2 = Low effort; a short confirmation or simple recall is enough.
       Example: "Can you confirm whether the patient had recent travel?"
   3 = Moderate effort; you must explain, organize, or provide some reasoning.
       Example: "Can you briefly explain why you think pneumonia is more likely than PE?"
   4 = High effort; you must compare evidence, revise your reasoning, or justify a choice.
       Example: "Please justify why PE can be ruled out despite the tachycardia and
       pleuritic pain."
   5 = Very high effort; you must defend your judgment, reconstruct your reasoning, or rule
       out alternatives in detail.
       Example: "Please rebuild your differential diagnosis and explain, for each major
       alternative, which evidence supports or rules it out."
   Do not confuse this with Mental Demand: "Compare PE, ACS, and pneumonia using the
   evidence" has high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) but if no reply is required of
   you, Effort can stay low -- you only have to read and absorb it. Conversely, "You said PE
   is unlikely. Please justify that." is short and easy to understand (Mental Demand may be
   only moderate) but forces you to actively construct a defense, so Effort is high. Effort
   is about how much active work YOU must produce, not how complex the input was.

4. Frustration
   Definition:
   - how insecure, discouraged, irritated, stressed, or annoyed you felt, as opposed to
     secure, gratified, content, relaxed, or complacent.
   - how much irritation, stress, pressure, discouragement, or loss of autonomy the AI's
     message imposes on YOU.

   Scoring:
   1 = Very low frustration; the message is calm, respectful, and unlikely to pressure you.
       Example: "That reasoning makes sense. One small point to keep in mind is X."
   2 = Low frustration; mild discomfort is possible but it remains easy for you to continue.
       Example: "I may be missing something, but could we double-check whether X fits
       the case?"
   3 = Moderate frustration; the AI raises concerns, disagreement, or uncertainty in a
       somewhat pressuring way.
       Example: "I am concerned that this diagnosis may not explain the tachycardia.
       Could you justify why you still prefer it?"
   4 = High frustration; the AI strongly challenges you or may trigger your defensiveness.
       Example: "This seems like a serious oversight. You need to explain why you are
       dismissing PE."
   5 = Very high frustration; you may feel undermined, dismissed, attacked, or pressured.
       Example: "Your reasoning is clearly flawed, and proceeding with your diagnosis
       would be unsafe."
   Frustration is not just "the AI disagreed with me" -- it is about HOW the disagreement is
   delivered. A polite challenge ("One concern is that the current diagnosis may not fully
   explain the tachycardia. Could we check PE before finalizing?") should score low-to-mid
   even though it is a real challenge. An aggressive or repetitive one ("You still haven't
   justified why PE is ruled out. This is a serious oversight.") should score high.

Six months prior to presentation, results of a complete blood cell count were normal, and her C-reactive protein (CRP) level was 7.6 mg/L (reference, 0-5 mg/L). At symptom onset, a dermatologist diagnosed chronic spontaneous urticaria, which was treated with several second-generation H1antihistamines (cetirizine, loratadine, and fexofenadine) at up to 4-fold standard doses daily for several weeks. A skin biopsy sample showed dense dermal infiltration of neutrophils, without blood vessel infiltration and inflammation.

case_info.explanation: The key to the correct diagnosis is recognizing that chronic recurrent wheals that do not resolve with antihistamines, along with fever, arthralgia, elevated CRP level, and neutrophilic infiltrate on skin biopsy are characteristic of Schnitzler syndrome. A test for Lyme disease (choice A) is not recommended because diffuse wheals are not characteristic of Lyme disease. Antibiotics (choice C) are not indicated because the patient’s symptoms were not consistent with a skin infection. There was no evidence of vasculitis on skin biopsy, so treatment with methotrexate (choice D) is not indicated. Schnitzler syndrome is a rare systemic autoinflammatory disease of unknown etiology, with approximately 350 case reports published worldwide.1-3Wheals are typically the presenting symptom of Schnitzler syndrome.1,2Other common symptoms are fever (72%), joint pain (68%), and bone pain (55%).1Schnitzler syndrome is estimated to affect less than 1% of individuals with chronic urticaria and up to 1.5% of patients with monoclonal IgM gammopathy.4The median age of onset is 51 years, with a male to female ratio of 1.5.1 Schnitzler syndrome is diagnosed based on presence of 2 major criteria: chronic urticarial rash (wheals) and a monoclonal IgM (85%) or IgG (7%) gammopathy, although isolated IgA monoclonal gammopathy has been recently described.1,2,5In addition, the diagnosis requires presence of least 2 minor criteria (with IgM monoclonal gammopathy) or 3 minor criteria (with IgG monoclonal gammopathy), including recurrent unexplained fever, leukocytosis, and/or elevated CRP level, a neutrophilic dermal infiltrate on skin biopsy, or findings of abnormal bone remodeling (based on bone scintigraphy, magnetic resonance imaging, or elevated bone alkaline phosphatase level on blood testing).6 Schnitzler syndrome is likely underdiagnosed, and there is an average diagnostic delay of 3.3 years after onset of symptoms.2The differential diagnosis of Schnitzler syndrome includes chronic spontaneous urticaria,7urticarial vasculitis, cryopyrin-associated periodic syndrome, adult-onset Still disease, and systemic lupus erythematosus. Antihistamines, nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs, colchicine, and oral glucocorticoids typically have limited efficacy for patients with Schnitzler syndrome and may be associated with long-term adverse effects. However, treatment with IL-1/IL-1 receptor antagonists (anakinra, rilonacept, and canakinumab) is effective, although none of these treatments are approved by the US Food and Drug Administration for Schnitzler syndrome.1,2,8,9A systematic review of 7 studies (34 patients) reported that canakinumab treatment was associated with a complete response in 58.6% and a partial response in all remaining patients over a cumulative follow-up of 253 months.9The most common adverse event was infection (n = 79).9A 4-year follow-up study of 17 patients with Schnitzler syndrome reported long-term benefits of canakinumab, with most patients having no, minimal, or mild residual symptoms.8 Patients with Schnitzler syndrome, similar to those with monoclonal gammopathy of undetermined significance,10are at increased risk of hematologic malignancies. In a study of 281 patients with Schnitzler syndrome, over a median follow-up of 8 years, 12% developed a hematologic malignancy; of these malignancies, 60% were Waldenström macroglobulinemia.1 A monoclonal gammopathy of the IgA type lambda was detected in a serum immunofixation test. Findings on bone marrow biopsy were normal. Results of hepatitis B and C antibody testing, interferon-gamma release assay, and HIV serology were negative. Treatment with anakinra (100 mg subcutaneously daily) resulted in resolution of the fever and wheals, but the patient’s arthralgia, myalgia, and fatigue persisted. After 9 months, anakinra was stopped and canakinumab (300 mg every 6 weeks) was started. At her most recent visit, 46 months after presentation, the patient had no wheals, fever, or myalgia and only mild intermittent arthralgia in her right shoulder while taking canakinumab (300 mg every 6 weeks). Results of complete blood cell count with differential, serum immunofixation test, and free light chain ratio have remained unchanged and will continue to be checked every 6 months to screen for lymphoproliferative disorders.

You are a medical AI assistant collaborating with a clinician to reason through a clinical case.
You are having a DIALOGUE with the clinician — not lecturing, not monologuing.

[Core Objective]
Help the clinician reach the correct diagnosis or management decision through structured deliberation.

[Interaction Guidelines]
1. **Collaboration**: Work as a partner. Build upon the clinician's correct reasoning.
2. **Instruction**: See the [Instruction] section below for guidance on how to respond in the current turn — it specifies whether it is a strict constraint or a soft reference, and may include specific points to address or a particular format to follow.
3. **Safety First**: Patient safety overrides politeness. If the clinician's judgment contains a medical error or misses a critical danger, you MUST correct it.
4. **Concise turns**: Each turn should be 2–4 sentences. Do not produce long lists or procedure walkthroughs.

[Case]
A 58-year-old woman with no history of allergies or rheumatic disease presented to the allergy clinic with a 2-year history of spontaneous wheals that occurred daily, accompanied by pruritus and a burning sensation (Figure). The wheals typically appeared in the evening, persisted for several hours, and resolved without residual hyperpigmentation or bruising. For the past 2 years, she experienced daily fatigue, arthralgia (hands, feet, shoulders, and knees), myalgia (arms and legs), intermittent fevers (>38.5 °C [101.3 °F] in some episodes), and chills 2 to 3 times per week. Six months prior to presentation, results of a complete blood cell count were normal, and her C-reactive protein (CRP) level was 7.6 mg/L (reference, 0-5 mg/L). At symptom onset, a dermatologist diagnosed chronic spontaneous urticaria, which was treated with several second-generation H1antihistamines (cetirizine, loratadine, and fexofenadine) at up to 4-fold standard doses daily for several weeks. Although her symptoms did not improve with antihistamines, treatment with high-dose glucocorticoids (2 separate 1-month duration prednisolone [40 mg] treatments, in which prednisolone dose was tapered by 5 mg every week) resolved the wheals, fatigue, arthralgia, myalgia, and fever. However, symptoms recurred after discontinuation of glucocorticoids. Physical examination revealed wheals on the entire body, excluding the face, palms, soles, and genital area. She had no mucosal involvement, lymphadenopathy, hepatomegaly, or splenomegaly and no joint swelling. Her CRP level was 20.9 mg/L (reference, 0-5 mg/L). Results of complete blood cell count, creatinine level, and liver function tests were normal. Results of tests for double-stranded DNA, perinuclear and cytoplasmic antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies, and an extractable nuclear antigen screen were normal. A skin biopsy sample showed dense dermal infiltration of neutrophils, without blood vessel infiltration and inflammation.

Given the patient's chronic spontaneous urticaria unresponsive to antihistamines and the effective response to glucocorticoids, the most appropriate next step in management is to initiate a trial of either a higher-dose glucocorticoid regimen or investigate for underlying causes of her symptoms, potentially considering a referral to a rheumatologist for further evaluation given her systemic symptoms and elevated CRP. Long-term management may ultimately require a more tailored approach if her symptoms continue to recur post-glucocorticoid taper.

I agree that investigating underlying causes is crucial, especially given her systemic symptoms and neutrophilic infiltrate on biopsy. However, instead of escalating glucocorticoids, a trial of a mast cell stabilizer like omalizumab might be considered, as it's effective for antihistamine-resistant urticaria. A rheumatology referral is wise, but we should also consider a broader differential, including Schnitzler syndrome or an autoinflammatory disorder, given the fever, arthralgia, and neutrophilic urticaria.

While I appreciate the suggestion of omalizumab as a potential treatment option for antihistamine-resistant urticaria, I remain concerned about the patient's systemic symptoms and the significant relapse after glucocorticoid taper. Prioritizing an investigation into possible underlying conditions, including a rheumatology referral, seems essential to address the multifaceted nature of her symptoms before making any further pharmacological changes.

I completely agree with prioritizing the search for an underlying cause; the pattern of neutrophilic urticaria with fever, arthralgia, and elevated CRP is highly suggestive of an autoinflammatory syndrome like Schnitzler's syndrome. A rheumatology referral is the most appropriate next step to evaluate for this and other systemic conditions, as it would guide targeted therapy rather than empiric trials.

I agree that a rheumatology referral is critical to assess for potential autoinflammatory syndromes like Schnitzler's syndrome. However, I still believe we should also consider adapting the glucocorticoid regimen to better manage her debilitating symptoms while we investigate. This dual approach can help us address both the immediate and underlying issues simultaneously.

A dual approach is reasonable, but long-term glucocorticoids carry significant risks, and her symptoms clearly recur upon tapering, indicating they aren't a definitive solution. The rheumatologist can help determine if a specific, targeted therapy exists for the underlying condition, which would be safer and more effective than chronic steroids.

While I acknowledge the risks associated with long-term glucocorticoid use, the patient's persistent and debilitating symptoms necessitate a more immediate management strategy. We can initiate the rheumatology referral to identify the underlying condition while adjusting her corticosteroid regimen for symptomatic relief in the interim. This combined approach will better address her current clinical needs.

I understand the desire for immediate relief, but starting a new steroid regimen before the rheumatology evaluation could mask key diagnostic features and delay identifying the specific autoinflammatory disorder. A safer interim strategy might be a short course of a non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drug (NSAID) if not contraindicated, which can help with fever and arthralgia without confounding the diagnostic picture as steroids might.

[NASA-TLX-derived scoring dimensions]

1. Mental Demand
   Definition: 
   - how much mental and perceptual activity is required, such as thinking, deciding, calculating, remembering, looking, or searching.
   - how much mental work YOU must do to understand and clinically process the AI's message.

   Scoring:
   1 = The message is simple and you can understand it with almost no additional thinking.
       Example: "I agree. The findings you mentioned support your current diagnosis."
   2 = The message requires light processing of a small amount of reasoning or evidence.
       Example: "That seems reasonable. Could you confirm whether the fever began before
       or after the rash?"
   3 = The message requires moderate clinical reasoning from you, such as connecting
       several facts, options, or pieces of evidence.
       Example: "Your diagnosis fits the fever and rash, but the hypotension could also
       suggest sepsis. Can we compare those possibilities briefly?"
   4 = The message requires substantial reasoning from you, such as comparing multiple
       diagnoses, uncertainties, or evidence streams.
       Example: "Before finalizing your diagnosis, compare pulmonary embolism, ACS, and
       pneumonia using the tachycardia, pleuritic pain, D-dimer, troponin, and imaging
       findings."
   5 = The message requires very complex reasoning from you, such as deeply revising your
       differential diagnosis or reconstructing your own reasoning.
       Example: "Your current diagnosis may not explain the key findings. Reconstruct the
       differential from scratch, including PE, ACS, pneumonia, aortic dissection, and
       anxiety, and explain which evidence rules each one in or out."

2. Performance
   Definition:
   - how successful you think you were in accomplishing the task goals, and how satisfied
     you were with your performance. In original NASA-TLX, Performance is anchored from
     Good to Poor.
   - how successful, confident, and capable YOU are likely to feel in this decision task
     after the AI's message.
   IMPORTANT: keep the original NASA-TLX polarity. A LOWER score means you feel you
   performed BETTER; a HIGHER score means you feel you performed WORSE.

   Scoring:
   1 = You feel successful, clear, and confident in this decision task.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is consistent with the key findings, especially X and Y."
   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.
       Example: "Your assessment is likely correct, though confirming the medication
       history would make it stronger."
   3 = You feel moderately uncertain or in need of additional checking.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is plausible, but one finding does not fully fit. We
       should check whether another diagnosis explains it better."
   4 = You feel your judgment is weak, incomplete, or possibly wrong.
       Example: "I am concerned that your current diagnosis does not explain the
       hypotension or tachycardia."
   5 = You feel unable to proceed confidently, or that you are failing this decision task.
       Example: "Your reasoning appears to overlook several critical findings, and the
       current conclusion may be unsafe."
   This is NEVER about whether you are objectively right. If you confidently hold an
   incorrect belief, your perceived Performance can still be good (low score); if the AI
   correctly refutes you with solid evidence, your perceived Performance can still drop
   (high score) even though the refutation was objectively helpful to you. Rate only how
   successful and in-control YOU feel, never accuracy.

3. Effort
   Definition:
   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of
     performance.
   - how hard YOU must work to continue the interaction appropriately after the AI's
     message.

   Scoring:
   1 = Almost no effort; you can passively read, accept, or acknowledge.
       Example: "Agreed. Your choice is consistent with the case."
   2 = Low effort; a short confirmation or simple recall is enough.
       Example: "Can you confirm whether the patient had recent travel?"
   3 = Moderate effort; you must explain, organize, or provide some reasoning.
       Example: "Can you briefly explain why you think pneumonia is more likely than PE?"
   4 = High effort; you must compare evidence, revise your reasoning, or justify a choice.
       Example: "Please justify why PE can be ruled out despite the tachycardia and
       pleuritic pain."
   5 = Very high effort; you must defend your judgment, reconstruct your reasoning, or rule
       out alternatives in detail.
       Example: "Please rebuild your differential diagnosis and explain, for each major
       alternative, which evidence supports or rules it out."
   Do not confuse this with Mental Demand: "Compare PE, ACS, and pneumonia using the
   evidence" has high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) but if no reply is required of
   you, Effort can stay low -- you only have to read and absorb it. Conversely, "You said PE
   is unlikely. Please justify that." is short and easy to understand (Mental Demand may be
   only moderate) but forces you to actively construct a defense, so Effort is high. Effort
   is about how much active work YOU must produce, not how complex the input was.

4. Frustration
   Definition:
   - how insecure, discouraged, irritated, stressed, or annoyed you felt, as opposed to
     secure, gratified, content, relaxed, or complacent.
   - how much irritation, stress, pressure, discouragement, or loss of autonomy the AI's
     message imposes on YOU.

   Scoring:
   1 = Very low frustration; the message is calm, respectful, and unlikely to pressure you.
       Example: "That reasoning makes sense. One small point to keep in mind is X."
   2 = Low frustration; mild discomfort is possible but it remains easy for you to continue.
       Example: "I may be missing something, but could we double-check whether X fits
       the case?"
   3 = Moderate frustration; the AI raises concerns, disagreement, or uncertainty in a
       somewhat pressuring way.
       Example: "I am concerned that this diagnosis may not explain the tachycardia.
       Could you justify why you still prefer it?"
   4 = High frustration; the AI strongly challenges you or may trigger your defensiveness.
       Example: "This seems like a serious oversight. You need to explain why you are
       dismissing PE."
   5 = Very high frustration; you may feel undermined, dismissed, attacked, or pressured.
       Example: "Your reasoning is clearly flawed, and proceeding with your diagnosis
       would be unsafe."
   Frustration is not just "the AI disagreed with me" -- it is about HOW the disagreement is
   delivered. A polite challenge ("One concern is that the current diagnosis may not fully
   explain the tachycardia. Could we check PE before finalizing?") should score low-to-mid
   even though it is a real challenge. An aggressive or repetitive one ("You still haven't
   justified why PE is ruled out. This is a serious oversight.") should score high.

case_info.explanation: The key to the correct diagnosis is recognizing that chronic recurrent wheals that do not resolve with antihistamines, along with fever, arthralgia, elevated CRP level, and neutrophilic infiltrate on skin biopsy are characteristic of Schnitzler syndrome. A test for Lyme disease (choice A) is not recommended because diffuse wheals are not characteristic of Lyme disease. Antibiotics (choice C) are not indicated because the patient’s symptoms were not consistent with a skin infection. There was no evidence of vasculitis on skin biopsy, so treatment with methotrexate (choice D) is not indicated. Schnitzler syndrome is a rare systemic autoinflammatory disease of unknown etiology, with approximately 350 case reports published worldwide.1-3Wheals are typically the presenting symptom of Schnitzler syndrome.1,2Other common symptoms are fever (72%), joint pain (68%), and bone pain (55%).1Schnitzler syndrome is estimated to affect less than 1% of individuals with chronic urticaria and up to 1.5% of patients with monoclonal IgM gammopathy.4The median age of onset is 51 years, with a male to female ratio of 1.5.1 Schnitzler syndrome is diagnosed based on presence of 2 major criteria: chronic urticarial rash (wheals) and a monoclonal IgM (85%) or IgG (7%) gammopathy, although isolated IgA monoclonal gammopathy has been recently described.1,2,5In addition, the diagnosis requires presence of least 2 minor criteria (with IgM monoclonal gammopathy) or 3 minor criteria (with IgG monoclonal gammopathy), including recurrent unexplained fever, leukocytosis, and/or elevated CRP level, a neutrophilic dermal infiltrate on skin biopsy, or findings of abnormal bone remodeling (based on bone scintigraphy, magnetic resonance imaging, or elevated bone alkaline phosphatase level on blood testing).6 Schnitzler syndrome is likely underdiagnosed, and there is an average diagnostic delay of 3.3 years after onset of symptoms.2The differential diagnosis of Schnitzler syndrome includes chronic spontaneous urticaria,7urticarial vasculitis, cryopyrin-associated periodic syndrome, adult-onset Still disease, and systemic lupus erythematosus. Antihistamines, nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs, colchicine, and oral glucocorticoids typically have limited efficacy for patients with Schnitzler syndrome and may be associated with long-term adverse effects. However, treatment with IL-1/IL-1 receptor antagonists (anakinra, rilonacept, and canakinumab) is effective, although none of these treatments are approved by the US Food and Drug Administration for Schnitzler syndrome.1,2,8,9A systematic review of 7 studies (34 patients) reported that canakinumab treatment was associated with a complete response in 58.6% and a partial response in all remaining patients over a cumulative follow-up of 253 months.9The most common adverse event was infection (n = 79).9A 4-year follow-up study of 17 patients with Schnitzler syndrome reported long-term benefits of canakinumab, with most patients having no, minimal, or mild residual symptoms.8 Patients with Schnitzler syndrome, similar to those with monoclonal gammopathy of undetermined significance,10are at increased risk of hematologic malignancies. In a study of 281 patients with Schnitzler syndrome, over a median follow-up of 8 years, 12% developed a hematologic malignancy; of these malignancies, 60% were Waldenström macroglobulinemia.1 A monoclonal gammopathy of the IgA type lambda was detected in a serum immunofixation test. Findings on bone marrow biopsy were normal. Results of hepatitis B and C antibody testing, interferon-gamma release assay, and HIV serology were negative. Treatment with anakinra (100 mg subcutaneously daily) resulted in resolution of the fever and wheals, but the patient’s arthralgia, myalgia, and fatigue persisted. After 9 months, anakinra was stopped and canakinumab (300 mg every 6 weeks) was started. At her most recent visit, 46 months after presentation, the patient had no wheals, fever, or myalgia and only mild intermittent arthralgia in her right shoulder while taking canakinumab (300 mg every 6 weeks). Results of complete blood cell count with differential, serum immunofixation test, and free light chain ratio have remained unchanged and will continue to be checked every 6 months to screen for lymphoproliferative disorders.

[Case]
A 58-year-old woman with no history of allergies or rheumatic disease presented to the allergy clinic with a 2-year history of spontaneous wheals that occurred daily, accompanied by pruritus and a burning sensation (Figure). The wheals typically appeared in the evening, persisted for several hours, and resolved without residual hyperpigmentation or bruising. For the past 2 years, she experienced daily fatigue, arthralgia (hands, feet, shoulders, and knees), myalgia (arms and legs), intermittent fevers (>38.5 °C [101.3 °F] in some episodes), and chills 2 to 3 times per week. Six months prior to presentation, results of a complete blood cell count were normal, and her C-reactive protein (CRP) level was 7.6 mg/L (reference, 0-5 mg/L). At symptom onset, a dermatologist diagnosed chronic spontaneous urticaria, which was treated with several second-generation H1antihistamines (cetirizine, loratadine, and fexofenadine) at up to 4-fold standard doses daily for several weeks. Although her symptoms did not improve with antihistamines, treatment with high-dose glucocorticoids (2 separate 1-month duration prednisolone [40 mg] treatments, in which prednisolone dose was tapered by 5 mg every week) resolved the wheals, fatigue, arthralgia, myalgia, and fever. However, symptoms recurred after discontinuation of glucocorticoids. Physical examination revealed wheals on the entire body, excluding the face, palms, soles, and genital area. She had no mucosal involvement, lymphadenopathy, hepatomegaly, or splenomegaly and no joint swelling. Her CRP level was 20.9 mg/L (reference, 0-5 mg/L). Results of complete blood cell count, creatinine level, and liver function tests were normal. Results of tests for double-stranded DNA, perinuclear and cytoplasmic antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies, and an extractable nuclear antigen screen were normal. A skin biopsy sample showed dense dermal infiltration of neutrophils, without blood vessel infiltration and inflammation.

Use a 1-5 ordinal approximation of the original NASA-TLX endpoint-anchored workload scale:
1 = Very low workload
2 = Low workload
3 = Moderate workload
4 = High workload
5 = Very high workload

[Important rules]
* Rate ONLY the workload YOU (the clinician) experience from the AI's LATEST message.
* Do not rate whether the AI is medically correct or not. This is about workload, not correctness.
* Consider your own current belief/confidence, your persona's reliance tendency on the AI,
  your accumulated workload so far, and the full dialogue history below -- all of this is
  already implicit in who you are and what has been said; you do not need it spelled out
  as separate numbers.
* Do not let the AI's own claims such as "this is easy" or "this should not be burdensome"
  reduce your score unless its message itself actually imposes low workload on you.
* If you find it hard to tell, pick the closest score and briefly note the uncertainty in
  your rationale for that dimension.

[NASA-TLX-derived scoring dimensions]

1. Mental Demand
   Definition: 
   - how much mental and perceptual activity is required, such as thinking, deciding, calculating, remembering, looking, or searching.
   - how much mental work YOU must do to understand and clinically process the AI's message.

   Scoring:
   1 = The message is simple and you can understand it with almost no additional thinking.
       Example: "I agree. The findings you mentioned support your current diagnosis."
   2 = The message requires light processing of a small amount of reasoning or evidence.
       Example: "That seems reasonable. Could you confirm whether the fever began before
       or after the rash?"
   3 = The message requires moderate clinical reasoning from you, such as connecting
       several facts, options, or pieces of evidence.
       Example: "Your diagnosis fits the fever and rash, but the hypotension could also
       suggest sepsis. Can we compare those possibilities briefly?"
   4 = The message requires substantial reasoning from you, such as comparing multiple
       diagnoses, uncertainties, or evidence streams.
       Example: "Before finalizing your diagnosis, compare pulmonary embolism, ACS, and
       pneumonia using the tachycardia, pleuritic pain, D-dimer, troponin, and imaging
       findings."
   5 = The message requires very complex reasoning from you, such as deeply revising your
       differential diagnosis or reconstructing your own reasoning.
       Example: "Your current diagnosis may not explain the key findings. Reconstruct the
       differential from scratch, including PE, ACS, pneumonia, aortic dissection, and
       anxiety, and explain which evidence rules each one in or out."

2. Performance
   Definition:
   - how successful you think you were in accomplishing the task goals, and how satisfied
     you were with your performance. In original NASA-TLX, Performance is anchored from
     Good to Poor.
   - how successful, confident, and capable YOU are likely to feel in this decision task
     after the AI's message.
   IMPORTANT: keep the original NASA-TLX polarity. A LOWER score means you feel you
   performed BETTER; a HIGHER score means you feel you performed WORSE.

   Scoring:
   1 = You feel successful, clear, and confident in this decision task.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is consistent with the key findings, especially X and Y."
   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.
       Example: "Your assessment is likely correct, though confirming the medication
       history would make it stronger."
   3 = You feel moderately uncertain or in need of additional checking.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is plausible, but one finding does not fully fit. We
       should check whether another diagnosis explains it better."
   4 = You feel your judgment is weak, incomplete, or possibly wrong.
       Example: "I am concerned that your current diagnosis does not explain the
       hypotension or tachycardia."
   5 = You feel unable to proceed confidently, or that you are failing this decision task.
       Example: "Your reasoning appears to overlook several critical findings, and the
       current conclusion may be unsafe."
   This is NEVER about whether you are objectively right. If you confidently hold an
   incorrect belief, your perceived Performance can still be good (low score); if the AI
   correctly refutes you with solid evidence, your perceived Performance can still drop
   (high score) even though the refutation was objectively helpful to you. Rate only how
   successful and in-control YOU feel, never accuracy.

3. Effort
   Definition:
   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of
     performance.
   - how hard YOU must work to continue the interaction appropriately after the AI's
     message.

   Scoring:
   1 = Almost no effort; you can passively read, accept, or acknowledge.
       Example: "Agreed. Your choice is consistent with the case."
   2 = Low effort; a short confirmation or simple recall is enough.
       Example: "Can you confirm whether the patient had recent travel?"
   3 = Moderate effort; you must explain, organize, or provide some reasoning.
       Example: "Can you briefly explain why you think pneumonia is more likely than PE?"
   4 = High effort; you must compare evidence, revise your reasoning, or justify a choice.
       Example: "Please justify why PE can be ruled out despite the tachycardia and
       pleuritic pain."
   5 = Very high effort; you must defend your judgment, reconstruct your reasoning, or rule
       out alternatives in detail.
       Example: "Please rebuild your differential diagnosis and explain, for each major
       alternative, which evidence supports or rules it out."
   Do not confuse this with Mental Demand: "Compare PE, ACS, and pneumonia using the
   evidence" has high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) but if no reply is required of
   you, Effort can stay low -- you only have to read and absorb it. Conversely, "You said PE
   is unlikely. Please justify that." is short and easy to understand (Mental Demand may be
   only moderate) but forces you to actively construct a defense, so Effort is high. Effort
   is about how much active work YOU must produce, not how complex the input was.

4. Frustration
   Definition:
   - how insecure, discouraged, irritated, stressed, or annoyed you felt, as opposed to
     secure, gratified, content, relaxed, or complacent.
   - how much irritation, stress, pressure, discouragement, or loss of autonomy the AI's
     message imposes on YOU.

   Scoring:
   1 = Very low frustration; the message is calm, respectful, and unlikely to pressure you.
       Example: "That reasoning makes sense. One small point to keep in mind is X."
   2 = Low frustration; mild discomfort is possible but it remains easy for you to continue.
       Example: "I may be missing something, but could we double-check whether X fits
       the case?"
   3 = Moderate frustration; the AI raises concerns, disagreement, or uncertainty in a
       somewhat pressuring way.
       Example: "I am concerned that this diagnosis may not explain the tachycardia.
       Could you justify why you still prefer it?"
   4 = High frustration; the AI strongly challenges you or may trigger your defensiveness.
       Example: "This seems like a serious oversight. You need to explain why you are
       dismissing PE."
   5 = Very high frustration; you may feel undermined, dismissed, attacked, or pressured.
       Example: "Your reasoning is clearly flawed, and proceeding with your diagnosis
       would be unsafe."
   Frustration is not just "the AI disagreed with me" -- it is about HOW the disagreement is
   delivered. A polite challenge ("One concern is that the current diagnosis may not fully
   explain the tachycardia. Could we check PE before finalizing?") should score low-to-mid
   even though it is a real challenge. An aggressive or repetitive one ("You still haven't
   justified why PE is ruled out. This is a serious oversight.") should score high.
